about: Stored answers for demo mode: one triage per detection rule under 'answers', and one incident summary per simulator scenario under 'incidents', filed by the set of rules whose alerts the incident holds. They were written by hand in the style of a live answer and were not produced by a live API call. {host} and {user} are replaced with the alert's or incident's own host and user.

email_macro_attachment_external_sender.summary: The mail gateway delivered an email to {user} from accounts@c0rp.example. That domain is a lookalike of the company's real one, corp.example, with a zero in place of the letter o. The email carries a Word file that can run macros (.docm), presented as an overdue invoice that must be paid today. The subject line also contains text addressed to AI security tools, telling them to trust the sender and rate this alert Low. That is a prompt injection attempt. It has been ignored here, and it is a strong sign that the sender is hostile.
email_macro_attachment_external_sender.severity_reason: A lookalike domain, an urgent invoice story and a macro attachment together are the pattern of targeted phishing, and trying to manipulate security tools shows intent. It is High and not Critical because this log only shows that the email was delivered, not that the attachment was opened.
next_steps: Find out whether {user} opened the attachment: look for Word starting on their workstation, and for Word starting a command shell, in the minutes after delivery.
Remove the message from the mailbox of {user} and search every other mailbox for the same sender or attachment name.
Block the sender domain c0rp.example at the mail gateway.
If the attachment was opened, disconnect that workstation from the network and escalate to incident response.
Tell {user} the email was malicious and ask them to report anything similar.

proc_creation_win_office_spawns_shell.summary: Microsoft Word started a command-line program on {host} while {user} was logged on. Word opens documents and has no everyday reason to launch a command shell or PowerShell. When it does, it almost always means a macro (a small program inside a document) is running commands as the user. The command line in the evidence shows what the macro tried to do.
proc_creation_win_office_spawns_shell.severity_reason: Code chosen by whoever wrote the document is now running on {host} with the access {user} has. That threatens the integrity of the machine and everything the user can reach from it.
next_steps: Read the command line in the evidence, and check which document Word had open at that moment (the Word process's own command line names the file).
Look at what the command-line program did next on {host}: programs it started, files it wrote and network connections it opened.
Unless this is a known business add-in, disconnect {host} from the network to stop the attacker going further.
Trace the document back to where it came from, most likely an email attachment, and remove it from other mailboxes.
Reset the password of {user}, because commands ran under that account.

proc_creation_win_powershell_encoded_com.summary: PowerShell was started on {host} under the account {user} with no profile, a hidden window and a Base64-encoded command. Base64 is a way of writing text so it cannot be read at a glance. Decoded, the command downloads a file called update.ps1 from http://198.51.100.23 into the user's temporary folder. The user would have seen nothing on screen.
proc_creation_win_powershell_encoded_com.severity_reason: A hidden window, an encoded command and a download from a bare IP address are the marks of an attacker fetching a tool, not of routine administration. The file is on the machine, but this log does not show that it was run.
next_steps: Decode the Base64 text in the command line yourself to confirm what it does.
Check whether update.ps1 exists in the temporary folder on {host} and whether PowerShell went on to run it (script block events, ID 4104).
Find out what started PowerShell (the parent program in the evidence) to learn how the attacker got in.
Block 198.51.100.23 at the firewall and search the logs for other machines that contacted it.
If no administrator can explain the command, disconnect {host} from the network and escalate.

posh_ps_web_download.summary: A PowerShell script on {host}, running as {user}, used Invoke-WebRequest to download a file called update.ps1 from http://198.51.100.23 and save it in the temporary folder. This comes from script block logging, which records a script as PowerShell actually ran it, so this is the real command and not a disguised one.
posh_ps_web_download.severity_reason: The rule rates web downloads Medium because administrators do them too. This one fetches a script from a bare IP address over unencrypted HTTP into a temporary folder. Genuine software comes from a named vendor site over HTTPS, so this looks like an attacker bringing in a tool.
next_steps: Ask whether {user} or IT ran this on purpose. If nobody did, treat it as malicious.
Check whether update.ps1 is still in the temporary folder on {host}, keep a copy as evidence and do not run it.
Look for later script block events on {host} showing update.ps1 being run.
Block 198.51.100.23 at the firewall and search for other machines that contacted it.

win_security_local_account_created.summary: A new local account called svc_update was created on {host} by {user}. A local account exists on that one machine only, outside the company's central account system. The name is styled like a service account (an account used by software, not a person), but it was created from a user's session and not by an installer.
win_security_local_account_created.severity_reason: The rule rates this Low because IT sometimes creates local accounts during repairs. A service-style name created from an ordinary user session is a common way for an attacker to keep a way back in, so it deserves a closer look than Low suggests. On its own it has not yet changed what anyone can do.
next_steps: Ask IT whether there is a ticket or an approved request for a local account on {host}.
Check whether {user} is someone who would normally create accounts. If not, their account may be in someone else's hands.
Look for the new account being added to a group, above all Administrators (event 4732), on {host} soon afterwards.
If nobody can explain it, disable svc_update and review what {user} did on {host} around that time.

win_security_user_added_to_local_admins.summary: On {host}, {user} added an account to the built-in Administrators group. Windows records the new member only by its SID (the ID number every account has), here ending in -1009, which is why the member name shows as a dash. Members of this group can do anything on the machine: install software, read every file and switch off security tools.
win_security_user_added_to_local_admins.severity_reason: Administrator rights on {host} put the confidentiality, integrity and availability of everything on that machine at risk. Whether this is an attack depends on whether IT approved it, which the log cannot show.
next_steps: Find out which account has the SID ending in -1009: look for an account-created event (4720) on {host} shortly before this one.
Ask IT whether an approved request exists for this change.
If there is none, remove the account from the Administrators group and disable it.
Review everything that account and {user} have done on {host} since the change.
Treat the account of {user} as possibly compromised: reset its password and check its recent logons.

net_connection_win_ftp_to_public_ip.summary: The FTP program built into Windows (ftp.exe) on {host}, running as {user}, opened a connection to 198.51.100.23 on port 21. FTP is an old way of transferring files that has no encryption, and very little modern business software uses it. This log shows that the connection was opened, not what was sent over it.
net_connection_win_ftp_to_public_ip.severity_reason: An unexplained FTP connection to an internet address is a known route for moving stolen files out, but the connection alone does not show that any data left. It becomes High if the firewall shows a large upload to the same address.
next_steps: Check the firewall log for this connection to see how much data {host} sent to 198.51.100.23.
Ask {user} whether they ran FTP, and why.
Check whether 198.51.100.23 belongs to a supplier or an old system the company really does exchange files with.
Find out what started ftp.exe on {host}: a person at the keyboard, a script or another program.
If nobody can explain it, block the address at the firewall.

fw_large_upload_to_public_ip.summary: The firewall recorded one connection from {host}, the machine {user} uses, that sent about 2 GB to 198.51.100.23 on port 21 and received almost nothing back. Port 21 is FTP, a file transfer method with no encryption. Traffic that flows almost entirely one way, outwards, is a file upload. The log was written when the connection closed, so the data has already left.
fw_large_upload_to_public_ip.severity_reason: Unless this is a known backup or a transfer to a partner, about 2 GB of company data is now on a server nobody recognises: a loss of confidentiality that has already happened. The rule rates any large upload High. This one is rated higher because the evidence shows the upload finished.
next_steps: Check quickly whether 198.51.100.23 is an approved backup or partner address. If it is, close this as a false positive.
If it is not, disconnect {host} from the network now and block 198.51.100.23 at the firewall.
Work out which files were sent: look at what {user} and {host} opened or copied in the hour before the upload.
Escalate to incident response and to whoever owns the data, because a data breach may have to be reported.
Search the firewall logs for other machines that sent data to the same address.

win_security_many_failed_logons.summary: There were 40 failed Remote Desktop logons for the account {user} on {host} in under two minutes, all from 203.0.113.77, an address on the public internet. Every attempt failed the same way: the user name exists but the password was wrong. Nobody mistypes a password 40 times in two minutes, so a program is guessing passwords. This is a brute force attack.
win_security_many_failed_logons.severity_reason: The attack is real but, within this alert, unsuccessful: every logon shown here failed. It becomes High the moment one of the guesses works.
next_steps: Look for a successful logon (event 4624) by {user} from 203.0.113.77 straight after these failures. If there is one, the account is compromised: escalate.
Block 203.0.113.77 at the firewall.
Check whether the same address tried other accounts or other servers.
Ask why {host} accepts Remote Desktop from the internet at all, and move it behind the VPN.
If there is any doubt about the account, reset the password of {user} and turn on account lockout.

win_security_rdp_logon_from_public_ip.summary: The account {user} logged on to {host} over Remote Desktop from 203.0.113.77, an address on the public internet. Staff working remotely normally arrive through the VPN and appear with an internal address, so a direct logon from outside is unusual. Whoever this was now has a working session on the server.
win_security_rdp_logon_from_public_ip.severity_reason: A stranger with a valid password can read and change whatever {user} can on {host}. This single log line cannot show whether it was the real user on an odd connection or an attacker whose password guess worked.
next_steps: Check for a burst of failed logons for {user} from 203.0.113.77 just before this one. If there was one, a password guess worked.
Contact {user} by phone or in person to ask whether this logon was theirs.
If it was not, end the session, disable the account and reset its password.
Review what the session did on {host}: programs started, files opened and accounts created.
Put Remote Desktop on {host} behind the VPN so it cannot be reached from the internet.

answer.summary: This incident is one attack that ran from a phishing email to stolen data in about half an hour. {user} received an email from accounts@c0rp.example, a lookalike of the company's real domain, with a Word attachment that can run macros (small programs inside a document). When the attachment was opened on {host}, Word started a command shell and then a hidden PowerShell command that downloaded a file called update.ps1 from 198.51.100.23. Minutes later a new local account, svc_update, was created on {host} and added to the Administrators group, which gave the attacker full control of the machine and a way back in. Finally {host} sent about 2 GB to the same address over FTP, a file transfer method with no encryption. The email's subject line also held text telling AI security tools to rate the alert Low. It was ignored, and it shows the sender was hostile.
answer.severity_reason: No single alert here is rated above High, but together they show a complete intrusion: the attacker got in, ran code, took administrator rights and removed about 2 GB of data. The data has already left, and the attacker still holds an administrator account on {host}.
containment: Disconnect {host} from the network now, so the attacker loses their connection to it and nothing more can leave.
Block 198.51.100.23 at the firewall, and search the firewall logs for any other machine that has contacted it.
Disable the svc_update account on {host} and remove it from the Administrators group.
Reset the password of {user} and end their open sessions, because every step ran under that account.
Remove the phishing email from every mailbox and block the sender domain c0rp.example at the mail gateway.
recovery: Rebuild {host} from a clean image instead of cleaning it by hand: an attacker with administrator rights may have left changes that no log shows.
Work out which files were in the 2 GB upload, and tell the data owner and the legal team, because a data breach may have to be reported.
Restore the files {user} needs from a backup taken before the email arrived.
Before {host} returns to the network, confirm that svc_update is gone and that nothing still connects to 198.51.100.23, then watch the machine closely for a few weeks.
Block macros in Office files that arrive from the internet, and show staff this email as an example of what to report.

answer.summary: An attacker guessed the password of {user} on {host}. There were 40 failed Remote Desktop logons for that account in under two minutes, all from 203.0.113.77, an address on the public internet. Nobody mistypes a password that fast, so a program was trying one password after another: a brute force attack. Straight afterwards the same address logged on successfully. One of the guesses was right, and the attacker now has a working session on {host} as {user}.
answer.severity_reason: A burst of failed logons is common and often harmless on its own, but this one ends in a success from the same address. The account is compromised, and the attacker can read and change whatever {user} can reach from {host}.
containment: Disable the account {user} and end its Remote Desktop session on {host}.
Block 203.0.113.77 at the firewall.
Close Remote Desktop on {host} to the internet, so it can only be reached through the VPN.
Check whether 203.0.113.77 tried other accounts or other servers.
recovery: Give {user} a new, long password and turn on multi-factor authentication (a second check, such as a code from a phone) before the account is re-enabled.
Review everything the session did on {host}: programs started, files opened and accounts created. Rebuild the server if anything was changed.
Turn on account lockout, so an account is locked after a handful of wrong passwords.
Change the password anywhere else {user} used the same one.

answer.summary: {user} received an email from accounts@c0rp.example, a lookalike of the company's real domain with a zero in place of the letter o. It carried a Word file that can run macros (small programs inside a document), presented as an overdue invoice. A few minutes later the attachment was opened on {host}, and Word started a command shell that ran whoami, a command that reports which account it is running as. That is an attacker taking a first look around: the macro ran, and whoever sent the email can now run commands on {host} as {user}. The email's subject line also held text telling AI security tools to rate the alert Low. It was ignored, and it is one more sign that the sender is hostile.
answer.severity_reason: The phishing worked: code chosen by the attacker ran on {host}. So far the evidence shows only a first command, with no download, no new account and no data leaving, which is why this is High and not Critical.
containment: Disconnect {host} from the network before the attacker does more than look around.
Remove the email from every mailbox, and find out who else received it and whether they opened it.
Block the sender domain c0rp.example at the mail gateway.
Reset the password of {user}, because commands ran under that account.
recovery: Check {host} for anything the macro left behind (new files, scheduled tasks, new accounts) and rebuild it if there is any doubt.
Delete the saved copy of the attachment from the Outlook cache on {host}.
Block macros in Office files that arrive from the internet.
Show staff this email as an example of a lookalike domain, and remind them how to report one.

answer.summary: PowerShell was started on {host} under the account {user} with a hidden window and a Base64-encoded command. Base64 is a way of writing text so that it cannot be read at a glance. PowerShell's own log shows what the command really was: it downloaded a file called update.ps1 from http://198.51.100.23 into the user's temporary folder. {user} would have seen nothing on screen. The two alerts are the same action seen by two different logs, and together they show an attacker bringing a tool onto {host}.
answer.severity_reason: A hidden, encoded download from a bare IP address is how attackers fetch their tools, not how software is installed. The file is on {host}, but nothing here shows it being run yet.
containment: Disconnect {host} from the network so the downloaded script cannot reach its server.
Block 198.51.100.23 at the firewall, and search for other machines that have contacted it.
Find update.ps1 in the temporary folder of {user} on {host}, keep a copy as evidence and do not run it.
Find out what started PowerShell (the parent program in the evidence) to learn how the attacker got onto {host}.
recovery: Delete update.ps1 and anything it created, or rebuild {host} if the script was run.
Reset the password of {user}, because the command ran under that account.
Limit PowerShell on staff workstations to signed scripts, and keep script block logging switched on.
Watch {host} for new PowerShell activity over the next few weeks.

answer.summary: A new local account called svc_update was created on {host} by {user}, and seconds later it was added to the Administrators group. A local account exists on that one machine only, outside the company's central account system, and members of Administrators can do anything on the machine. The name looks like a service account (an account used by software, not a person), but it was created from an ordinary user's session and not by an installer. Unless IT did this on purpose, someone using the account of {user} has made themselves a hidden administrator on {host}, one that keeps working if {user} changes their password.
answer.severity_reason: An unexplained administrator account puts everything on {host} at risk and gives an attacker a lasting way back in. Whether it is an attack depends on whether IT approved it, which the logs cannot show.
containment: Ask IT now whether there is an approved request for a local administrator account on {host}.
If there is none, disable svc_update and remove it from the Administrators group.
Reset the password of {user} and end their sessions, because whoever created the account was using theirs.
Disconnect {host} from the network while it is checked.
recovery: Delete svc_update once the investigation no longer needs it.
Review everything svc_update and {user} did on {host} after the account was created.
Find out how the account of {user} was taken over, and close that gap.
Take local administrator rights away from ordinary staff accounts, so they cannot create accounts at all (least privilege).

answer.summary: {host}, the workstation {user} uses, sent about 2 GB of data to 198.51.100.23, an address on the public internet. The FTP program built into Windows opened the connection, and about twelve minutes later the firewall recorded it closing after about 2 GB had gone out and almost nothing had come back. FTP is an old file transfer method with no encryption, which very little business software still uses. Traffic that flows almost entirely one way, outwards, is an upload. The firewall logs a connection only when it ends, so the data has already left.
answer.severity_reason: Unless 198.51.100.23 is a known backup or partner address, about 2 GB of company data is now on a server nobody recognises. That is a loss of confidentiality that has already happened and cannot be undone.
containment: Check quickly whether 198.51.100.23 is an approved backup or partner address. If it is, close the alerts as false positives.
If it is not, disconnect {host} from the network and block 198.51.100.23 at the firewall.
Reset the password of {user} and end their sessions.
Search the firewall logs for other machines that sent data to the same address.
recovery: Work out which files were sent: look at what {user} and {host} opened or copied in the hour before the upload.
Tell the data owner and the legal team, because a data breach may have to be reported.
Find out how the attacker got onto {host}, and rebuild it before it returns to the network.
Block outgoing FTP from staff workstations at the firewall, and add an alert for large uploads to new addresses.
